screens.title: Setting Up Asynchronous Replication
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to build a basic asynchronous replication link between a MySQL source and a replica. We'll emphasize the exact configuration steps that must be present on every server: a unique server identifier, binary logging on the source, recommended ROW binlog format, and a restricted replication user. You will see how to take a consistent data snapshot using mysqldump with the single-transaction and master-data options, why flushing binary logs matters for creating reliable starting coordinates, and how to apply those coordinates on the replica with CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO followed by START REPLICA. I will also preview common mistakes you will want to avoid, such as duplicate server_id values and wrong log file positions, and how to verify success with SHOW REPLICA STATUS. By the end of the chapter you will be able to configure a source and a replica, perform the initial synchronization, start replication, and validate that the replica is receiving and applying events correctly. Consider this your practical checklist for a safe initial replication setup.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Setting Up Asynchronous Replication
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Setting Up Asynchronous Replication

A hands-on walkthrough: configure source and replica, capture a consistent snapshot, and start replication with verification and troubleshooting guidance.

In this lesson
Prerequisites, source config, snapshot with mysqldump, replica configuration, start and verify replication.
Core commands
my.cnf edits, CREATE USER / GRANT, mysqldump, CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO, START REPLICA, SHOW REPLICA STATUS.
Verify
Look for Replica_IO_Running and Replica_SQL_Running set to Yes and no recent errors.
Explore Key Topics
Source configuration
Enable log_bin and set a unique server_id; ROW format recommended for consistency.
Consistent snapshot
Use mysqldump with --single-transaction and --master-data=2 to capture binlog coordinates.
Replica start
Apply CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO with the dump's binlog file and position, then START REPLICA.
Concept map
Source → Snapshot → Replica → Verify
Server IDs
Every server needs a unique integer server_id to avoid loops.
Binlog format
ROW format is recommended for accurate replication of non-deterministic operations.
Check
SHOW REPLICA STATUS should report both IO and SQL threads running.

screens.title: Prerequisites for a Successful Replica
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable replication setup starts with clear prerequisites. First, every server in the topology must have a unique server_id: this integer is how MySQL tags events and prevents replication loops. For example, using server_id 1 for the source and server_id 2 for the replica is a minimal safe pattern. Second, the source server must have binary logging enabled via log_bin because replication depends entirely on the binary log events the replica will read. Third, choose binlog_format ROW when possible; ROW records row changes and avoids many consistency problems that can arise with statement-based replication, especially for non-deterministic or complex queries. Fourth, verify network connectivity on the MySQL port between source and replica and ensure firewalls or cloud security groups allow the traffic. A common misconception is that replication will work without unique IDs or with log_bin disabled; it will not. As a quick check, after restarting MySQL you should run SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'server_id'; and SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_bin';. Why do these prerequisites matter? They are the foundation that guarantees the replica can receive a complete and ordered sequence of events to reproduce the source's changes accurately.

keyIdea.title: Prerequisites first
keyIdea.text: Unique server_id and binary logging on the source are non-negotiable; ROW binlog format and open network access reduce replication failure modes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Prerequisites for a Successful Replica
Definition and why it matters
  • Unique server_id: prevents replication loops and correctly attributes events to their origin.
  • log_bin on source: without it, there are no events for replicas to consume.
  • binlog_format=ROW: recommended for consistency with complex or non-deterministic operations.
  • Network & firewall: replicas must be able to reach the source on MySQL's port.
Common misconception
Thinking server_id can be omitted or duplicated. If duplicated, replication loops or ignored events can occur.
Key Takeaway

Confirm server_id uniqueness and enable log_bin with ROW format before any dump or replica configuration.

Quick checks and commands
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'server_id';
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_bin';
# Ensure port 3306 is reachable between servers before proceeding
Example: pick small integers for IDs during testing (1 for source, 2 for replica), but keep them unique in production topologies where more nodes exist.
Why this fills the gap
These checks stop expensive mistakes later. If you miss enabling binlogs or use duplicated IDs, replication will fail or produce inconsistent results.

screens.title: Configuring the Source Server (my.cnf)
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring the source server is a precise, repeatable step. You will edit my. cnf under the [mysqld] section to enable binary logging and to set a unique server_id and binlog_format. The chapter supplies a standard snippet: log_bin = mysql-bin, server_id = 1, binlog_format = ROW, and optional housekeeping settings like expire_logs_days and max_binlog_size. After saving the file you must restart the MySQL service so the server reads the updated variables. A quick verification step is to run SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_bin'; and SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'server_id'; to confirm the values. A common mistake is to forget the restart or to edit the wrong my. cnf file; always confirm which file your distribution uses and then verify the running variables. In practice, enabling ROW avoids subtle replication anomalies and the expire_logs_days setting helps control disk consumption of binlogs. This configuration is the foundation for creating a reliable event stream your replicas will follow. Configuring the Source Server (my.cnf) means make deterministic my.cnf edits, restart mysql, and immediately verify the server variables to ensure binary logging and server_id are active.. In practical terms, edit my.cnf, enable binary logging, set server_id and binlog format. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Make deterministic my.cnf edits, restart MySQL, and immediately verify the server variables to ensure binary logging and server_id are active.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Configuring the Source Server (my.cnf)
my.cnf example
[mysqld]
log_bin = mysql-bin             # Enables binary logging and sets base name
server_id = 1                   # Unique ID for this server
binlog_format = ROW             # Recommended for consistency
expire_logs_days = 7            # Purge binlogs older than 7 days
max_binlog_size = 100M          # Max size of a single binlog file
After editing, restart MySQL using your system's service manager, then run the variable checks to confirm values are active. Do not skip verification — the server must report the settings at runtime.
Explanation and pitfalls
  • log_bin creates the event stream replicas read; without it, replication is impossible.
  • server_id must be unique across all servers to avoid misattributed events or loops.
  • binlog_format ROW captures exact row changes and reduces replication anomalies.
  • Common pitfall: editing a different configuration file than the one MySQL loads—always verify with SHOW VARIABLES.
Pro tip
Document your my.cnf changes and keep a versioned copy to simplify rollbacks during testing.

screens.title: Creating a Dedicated Replication User
screens.narratorSegment: A dedicated replication user is the secure channel by which the replica connects to the source to fetch binary log events. The recommended privileges are narrowly scoped: grant REPLICATION SLAVE only. The chapter example shows creating repl_user bound to the replica IP address and granting the necessary privilege, followed by FLUSH PRIVILEGES. Restricting the user to the replica's IP reduces risk compared with allowing connections from everywhere. A common mistake is granting broad privileges or using a root-level account, which exposes the source to accidental modifications or a larger attack surface. After creating the user, test connectivity from the replica host and ensure the credentials work for a connection to the source MySQL port. Remember to choose a strong password and to avoid storing it in plain text where it can be exposed. This minimal, host-restricted account model keeps replication secure and auditable while providing the replica the access it needs. Creating a Dedicated Replication User means create a replication slave user restricted by replica ip and test connectivity before starting the replication threads.. In practical terms, least-privilege replication slave user bound to the replica host. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Creating a Dedicated Replication User
SQL example (on the source)
CREATE USER 'repl_user'@'192.168.1.101' IDENTIFIED BY 'YourStrongPassword!';
GRANT REPLICATION SLAVE ON *.* TO 'repl_user'@'192.168.1.101';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;
Replace the host with the replica's IP. For multiple replicas you may create one user per replica or employ a controlled wildcard with caution.
Why this design matters
  • Least privilege reduces the impact of credential compromise.
  • Binding the user to a specific IP prevents other hosts from authenticating with the same credentials.
  • Testing the credentials from the replica helps catch network or permission issues before starting replication.
Check
From the replica host, verify you can connect to the source using the replication user credentials before applying the CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO statement.

screens.title: Taking a Consistent Snapshot with mysqldump
screens.narratorSegment: A consistent snapshot establishes the exact data state and the starting point in the binary log for the replica to follow. The recommended mysqldump invocation includes --single-transaction, which opens a consistent InnoDB snapshot without locking all tables, and --flush-logs, which rotates the binary log to ensure the recorded file and position are clean. The --master-data=2 option causes mysqldump to include a commented CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO line that contains the SOURCE_LOG_FILE and SOURCE_LOG_POS values you will later use on the replica. The chapter example shows dumping all databases to full_backup. sql. After the dump finishes, inspect the file for the commented CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO line to extract the binlog file and position. A common misconception is that locking tables is required for InnoDB; instead, single-transaction achieves a consistent snapshot without broad locks. Always transfer the dump file to the replica securely and keep the binlog values handy for the next step. Taking a Consistent Snapshot with mysqldump means mysqldump with --single-transaction --flush-logs --master-data=2 yields a consistent data snapshot and the binlog coordinates needed to start the replica precisely.. In practical terms, use --single-transaction, --flush-logs, and --master-data=2 to capture data and binlog coordinates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: mysqldump with --single-transaction --flush-logs --master-data=2 yields a consistent data snapshot and the binlog coordinates needed to start the replica precisely.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Taking a Consistent Snapshot with mysqldump
mysqldump command
mysqldump -u root -p --all-databases --single-transaction --flush-logs --master-data=2 > /tmp/full_backup.sql
Key options: --single-transaction for InnoDB consistency, --flush-logs to rotate binlogs, and --master-data=2 to capture the binlog file and position in the dump output.
After the dump
Open /tmp/full_backup.sql and find the commented CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO line to extract SOURCE_LOG_FILE and SOURCE_LOG_POS.
Explanation cards
Consistent snapshot without locks for InnoDB using single-transaction.
Flush logs creates a new binary log so the dump records a clean start point.
Master-data=2 writes commented replica-start coordinates you will later use verbatim.

screens.title: Transfer and Import the Snapshot on the Replica
screens.narratorSegment: Once you have the consistent dump file, transfer it to the replica server using a secure method. The chapter simply states to 'securely transfer' the file; in practice, ensure the transport preserves confidentiality and integrity. After the file is on the replica, import it with the mysql client. The command in the chapter is mysql -u root -p < full_backup. sql which restores the dumped databases and applies the initial data state that matches the binlog coordinates recorded in the dump. After import completes, the replica's data set will match the source at the time of the dump. A common mistake is to start replication before importing the dump or to use mismatched binlog coordinates that do not correspond to the imported snapshot. Always import first, then configure replication with values taken from the dump. This sequencing prevents data divergence and ensures the replica applies events starting exactly from the dump's recorded point. Transfer and Import the Snapshot on the Replica means import the consistent dump to the replica before applying change replication source to so the data and the binlog coordinates align exactly.. In practical terms, move the dump file securely, then import to populate the replica. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Transfer and Import the Snapshot on the Replica
Import command (on the replica)
mysql -u root -p < /path/to/full_backup.sql
This command loads the database state captured by the dump so the replica starts with the same data as the source at the dump time.
Key Takeaway

Always import the dump before configuring replication so the replica's data aligns with the binlog coordinates you will supply.

Transfer considerations & checklist
  • Use a secure transport method to move the dump to the replica (the chapter recommends secure transfer without prescribing a tool).
  • Confirm file integrity on the replica before import.
  • Do not start replication until the import completes and you have the dump's SOURCE_LOG_FILE and SOURCE_LOG_POS.

screens.title: Configure and Start the Replica
screens.narratorSegment: After importing the dump and ensuring the replica has a unique server_id and optional read_only setting, you will tell the replica where to start reading events from the source. Use CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO, providing SOURCE_HOST, SOURCE_USER, SOURCE_PASSWORD, SOURCE_LOG_FILE, and SOURCE_LOG_POS based on the mysqldump output or SHOW MASTER STATUS recorded immediately after the dump. The chapter gives a template that you should replace with your actual values, then execute START REPLICA. Starting the replica creates two threads: the IO thread, which connects to the source and reads binary events, and the S Q L thread, which applies those events locally. A frequent error is to supply incorrect SOURCE_LOG_FILE or SOURCE_LOG_POS values that do not match the imported snapshot; this will cause replication to fail. Ensure credentials are correct and that the source allows connections from the replica's IP. After starting, use SHOW REPLICA STATUS to confirm both IO and S Q L threads are running. Configure and Start the Replica means initialize the replica with the exact source_log_file and source_log_pos from your dump, then start replication and confirm both replication threads are running.. In practical terms, use change replication source to with the dump's coordinates, then start replica. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Replica configuration template
CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO
  SOURCE_HOST='source_ip_address',
  SOURCE_USER='repl_user',
  SOURCE_PASSWORD='YourStrongPassword!',
  SOURCE_LOG_FILE='mysql-bin.00000X',
  SOURCE_LOG_POS=YYYY;

START REPLICA;
Replace the host, user, password, and the binlog file and position you extracted from the dump. Then run START REPLICA to begin replication.
What to watch for
  • Replica_IO_Running: Yes — IO thread can connect and read events.
  • Replica_SQL_Running: Yes — SQL thread is applying events.
  • Empty Last_IO_Error and Last_SQL_Error indicate no immediate failures.
Quick check
If either thread is No, inspect the connection details, credentials, and the binlog file/position you supplied.

screens.title: Verifying Replication Status
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is the final guardrail in the initial setup. SHOW REPLICA STATUS returns many fields, but the chapter highlights a few critical ones: Replica_IO_Running and Replica_SQL_Running should both report Yes. Last_IO_Error and Last_SQL_Error should be empty. Seconds_Behind_Source reports how far the S Q L thread is behind the source; ideally it is zero or very small. If Replica_IO_Running is No, the replica cannot connect to the source — the two most likely causes are a firewall blocking port 3306 or an incorrect SOURCE_HOST in the CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO command. If Replica_SQL_Running is No, examine S Q L errors that may arise from incompatible data or missing objects. Always consult the MySQL error log on the affected server for more details. A misconception to avoid is assuming a nonzero Seconds_Behind_Source always indicates a problem — short-lived lags can be normal under load. Your goal is to confirm both threads are running and error fields are empty as a first validation of success. Verifying Replication Status means confirm replica_io_running and replica_sql_running are yes, error fields are empty, and seconds_behind_source is acceptable for your workload.. In practical terms, use show replica status to confirm threads, lag, and absence of errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Common Setup Issues and How to Troubleshoot
screens.narratorSegment: When initial replication fails, the chapter lists the most frequent culprits and how to approach them. The first and most common error is a connection failure indicated by Replica_IO_Running: No and Last_IO_Error stating that the source is unreachable. The two most likely causes are a firewall blocking port 3306 and an incorrect SOURCE_HOST or IP. Begin troubleshooting by checking firewall rules and attempting a basic network connection from the replica to the source on the MySQL port. The second common failure is supplying the wrong SOURCE_LOG_FILE or SOURCE_LOG_POS that do not match the imported snapshot; this leads to inconsistent or failing replication. If this happens, re-extract coordinates from the dump or take a fresh snapshot. Another frequent issue is duplicated server_id values; this causes event attribution problems and must be fixed by assigning unique IDs. Finally, incorrect replication user credentials or host restrictions will prevent the IO thread from authenticating. Always consult the MySQL error logs on both servers for detailed diagnostics and stop replication before making major changes. Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Common Setup Issues and How to Troubleshoot
Can't connect
Replica_IO_Running No with Last_IO_Error about connection. Likely firewall or wrong SOURCE_HOST. Verify network reachability and security group rules.
Bad coordinates
Supplying SOURCE_LOG_FILE/POS that don't match the imported snapshot causes replication to fail. Re-extract from dump or take a new snapshot.
Credential or host restriction
Incorrect replication user or wrong host restriction prevents authentication. Check GRANTs and test connection from the replica host.
server_id conflicts
Duplicate server_id values disrupt event attribution. Ensure each server has a distinct integer server_id.
Logs tell the story
Consult the MySQL error log on the source and replica for precise failure messages before making changes.
Safe procedures
Stop replication before major changes using STOP REPLICA; then correct configuration and restart the threads.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Activity: Initialize a Replica from a Source with mysqldump
Scenario
Source: 192.168.1.100, Replica: 192.168.1.101. Assume source has log_bin and server_id=1 and a replication user exists.
Step 1 — Dump on source
mysqldump -u root -p --all-databases --single-transaction --flush-logs --master-data=2 > /tmp/full_backup.sql

Transfer the dump to the replica and import:
mysql -u root -p < /path/to/full_backup.sql
Construct CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO using the extracted SOURCE_LOG_FILE and SOURCE_LOG_POS, then START REPLICA and run SHOW REPLICA STATUS to confirm success.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to build a basic asynchronous replication link between a MySQL source and a replica. We'll emphasize the exact configuration steps that must be present on every server: a unique server identifier, binary logging on the source, recommended ROW binlog format, and a restricted replication user. You will see how to take a consistent data snapshot using mysqldump with the single-transaction and master-data options, why flushing binary logs matters for creating reliable starting coordinates, and how to apply those coordinates on the replica with CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO followed by START REPLICA. I will also preview common mistakes you will want to avoid, such as duplicate server_id values and wrong log file positions, and how to verify success with SHOW REPLICA STATUS. By the end of the chapter you will be able to configure a source and a replica, perform the initial synchronization, start replication, and validate that the replica is receiving and applying events correctly. Consider this your practical checklist for a safe initial replication setup.

In this chapter you will practice and verify the full initial setup for asynchronous replication. First, you will identify essential prerequisites such as unique server_id values and enabling binary logging on the source. This matters because replication depends on event streams in the binary log and unique identifiers to avoid loops. Second, you will configure the source: edit the my. cnf to enable log_bin, set binlog_format to ROW, and create a privileged-but-restricted replication user; each of these steps keeps the replication link secure and consistent. Third, you will perform a consistent snapshot using mysqldump with --single-transaction and --master-data=2 so the replica starts from a precise binlog file and position. Finally, you will configure and start the replica using CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO followed by START REPLICA and verify with SHOW REPLICA STATUS. Each objective emphasizes why the step matters and what to check to avoid common mistakes in production.

This second set of objectives focuses on practical skills you will perform and how to reason about them. You will configure my. cnf on both source and replica, restart the MySQL service, and validate the server variables that control replication. Practically, checking SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_bin' and SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'server_id' confirms your edits took effect. You will also learn to create a dedicated replication user with only REPLICATION SLAVE privileges restricted by host address, reducing attack surface and accidental access. Finally, you will practice reading the mysqldump output to extract the SOURCE_LOG_FILE and SOURCE_LOG_POS values, and then apply them in CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO before starting replication. Each skill is paired with a reason: verification prevents missed steps, least-privilege reduces risk, and precise coordinates stop data gaps or duplication. These competencies are what you will be expected to demonstrate in the hands-on activity.

A reliable replication setup starts with clear prerequisites. First, every server in the topology must have a unique server_id: this integer is how MySQL tags events and prevents replication loops. For example, using server_id 1 for the source and server_id 2 for the replica is a minimal safe pattern. Second, the source server must have binary logging enabled via log_bin because replication depends entirely on the binary log events the replica will read. Third, choose binlog_format ROW when possible; ROW records row changes and avoids many consistency problems that can arise with statement-based replication, especially for non-deterministic or complex queries. Fourth, verify network connectivity on the MySQL port between source and replica and ensure firewalls or cloud security groups allow the traffic. A common misconception is that replication will work without unique IDs or with log_bin disabled; it will not. As a quick check, after restarting MySQL you should run SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'server_id'; and SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_bin';. Why do these prerequisites matter? They are the foundation that guarantees the replica can receive a complete and ordered sequence of events to reproduce the source's changes accurately.

Configuring the source server is a precise, repeatable step. You will edit my. cnf under the [mysqld] section to enable binary logging and to set a unique server_id and binlog_format. The chapter supplies a standard snippet: log_bin = mysql-bin, server_id = 1, binlog_format = ROW, and optional housekeeping settings like expire_logs_days and max_binlog_size. After saving the file you must restart the MySQL service so the server reads the updated variables. A quick verification step is to run SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_bin'; and SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'server_id'; to confirm the values. A common mistake is to forget the restart or to edit the wrong my. cnf file; always confirm which file your distribution uses and then verify the running variables. In practice, enabling ROW avoids subtle replication anomalies and the expire_logs_days setting helps control disk consumption of binlogs. This configuration is the foundation for creating a reliable event stream your replicas will follow. Configuring the Source Server (my.cnf) means make deterministic my.cnf edits, restart mysql, and immediately verify the server variables to ensure binary logging and server_id are active.. In practical terms, edit my.cnf, enable binary logging, set server_id and binlog format. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A dedicated replication user is the secure channel by which the replica connects to the source to fetch binary log events. The recommended privileges are narrowly scoped: grant REPLICATION SLAVE only. The chapter example shows creating repl_user bound to the replica IP address and granting the necessary privilege, followed by FLUSH PRIVILEGES. A consistent snapshot establishes the exact data state and the starting point in the binary log for the replica to follow. The recommended mysqldump invocation includes --single-transaction, which opens a consistent InnoDB snapshot without locking all tables, and --flush-logs, which rotates the binary log to ensure the recorded file and position are clean. The --master-data=2 option causes mysqldump to include a commented CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO line that contains the SOURCE_LOG_FILE and SOURCE_LOG_POS values you will later use on the replica. Verification is the final guardrail in the initial setup. SHOW REPLICA STATUS returns many fields, but the chapter highlights a few critical ones: Replica_IO_Running and Replica_SQL_Running should both report Yes. Last_IO_Error and Last_SQL_Error should be empty. Seconds_Behind_Source reports how far the S Q L thread is behind the source; ideally it is zero or very small. If Replica_IO_Running is No, the replica cannot connect to the source — the two most likely causes are a firewall blocking port 3306 or an incorrect SOURCE_HOST in the CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO command. When initial replication fails, the chapter lists the most frequent culprits and how to approach them. The first and most common error is a connection failure indicated by Replica_IO_Running: No and Last_IO_Error stating that the source is unreachable. The two most likely causes are a firewall blocking port 3306 and an incorrect SOURCE_HOST or IP. Begin troubleshooting by checking firewall rules and attempting a basic network connection from the replica to the source on the MySQL port. The second common failure is supplying the wrong SOURCE_LOG_FILE or SOURCE_LOG_POS that do not match the imported snapshot; this leads to inconsistent or failing replication. If this happens, re-extract coordinates from the dump or take a fresh snapshot. Another frequent issue is duplicated server_id values; this causes event attribution problems and must be fixed by assigning unique IDs. Finally, incorrect replication user credentials or host restrictions will prevent the IO thread from authenticating. Always consult the MySQL error logs on both servers for detailed diagnostics and stop replication before making major changes. These three core settings underlie a correct replication setup. First, server_id is a unique integer per server that prevents event loops and ensures events are correctly attributed. Second, log_bin must be enabled on the source because binary logging is the event stream replicas read; without it replication cannot function. Third, binlog_format set to ROW is recommended to capture actual row changes and avoid anomalies with non-deterministic statements. Keep these three ideas in mind whenever you plan a replication topology: they are the minimal, non-negotiable configuration elements. A quick reflection: if any of these are misconfigured, replication will either fail to start or produce inconsistent results, so always verify them before proceeding to snapshot and start the replica.
